body_markdown:
Who is the employer when you outsource payroll?
When you outsource payroll and related tax duties to a third-party payer, the IRS says you will generally remain responsible for those duties, including liability for the taxes. The exception is a certified professional employer organization (CPEO), which is treated as the employer of a worksite employee for federal employment taxes, but only for pay the CPEO remits to that employee.
Who counts as the employer under the IRS common-law test?
The IRS applies a common-law test. A business is the employer when it can control what work is done and how it is done, even if it gives the worker freedom of action. IRS Publication 15 adds that the name given to the relationship does not decide whether an employer-employee relationship exists.


Two questions run through every arrangement below. Who directs the work, and whose employer identification number (EIN) appears on the returns?
What changes when you run payroll in software?
An employer that runs its own payroll is the common law employer, and the IRS describes a common law employer as one that withholds and files its own employment tax returns and Forms W-2 and W-3, and obtains its own EIN for that purpose. The IRS test turns on the right to control the work, so running payroll in software does not change who the employer is.
What changes with managed payroll?
In managed payroll, a provider’s specialists run payroll for the employer. The IRS says what that does to liability depends on the type of third-party arrangement.


A payroll service provider may prepare paychecks, prepare and file employment tax returns, prepare Forms W-2, and make federal tax deposits and other federal tax payments for the employer. A reporting agent, authorized on Form 8655, signs and generally e-files returns separately under each client’s EIN and may deposit and pay on the client’s behalf. A payroll service provider or reporting agent works under the employer’s own EIN, and the IRS says neither is liable as an employer or an agent for the employer’s employment taxes.


Under the general rule, the employer stays responsible for returns, deposits and payments if the third party fails to perform a required action. If the third party fails to make the deposits and payments, the IRS may assess penalties and interest on the employer’s account. A reporting agent must also give its client a written statement when the contract starts and at least quarterly, saying the client remains responsible for timely filing and payment.
What changes with a PEO arrangement?
The IRS describes a PEO as an organization that agrees with a client to perform some or all of the client’s federal employment tax withholding, reporting and payment functions, and that may also manage human resources, benefits, workers compensation claims and unemployment insurance claims. In industry usage, a PEO is a co-employment model. That phrase describes the model and is not a tax status, because the IRS says the Internal Revenue Code does not define “co-employer” and the concept is not recognized under federal tax law.


The IRS looks at the facts of the arrangement. In the PEO arrangement the IRS describes, the client typically remains the common law employer, and a PEO that is merely a conduit for the funds used to pay wages is not the section 3401(d)(1) employer, which is the person with control of wage payment. To decide whether a client is the common law employer, the IRS reviews whether the client directs the day-to-day duties of the workers, retains the authority to hire and fire, and sets pay.


Treasury Regulation 31.3504-2 adds a separate test for a payor that pays wages under a service agreement. A service agreement is one in which the payor asserts it is the employer, pays the wages and assumes responsibility for the taxes, and all three elements are required. The regulation uses the word co-employer only as one way a payor can assert employer status. A PEO that is not a CPEO and meets that definition is designated to perform employer acts for the wages it pays, and the IRS says the PEO and its client are concurrently liable. Under the same regulation, a payor is not designated for wages that are reported on a return filed under the client’s EIN.


The IRS also says state PEO laws have no bearing on the determination of liability for federal employment tax purposes.
What changes when the PEO is certified?
The CPEO program is a voluntary IRS certification for PEOs. Under Internal Revenue Code section 3511, a CPEO is treated as the employer of a worksite employee for federal employment taxes, but only for pay the CPEO remits to that employee. Under section 7705(e) of the Code, a worksite employee is an individual who performs services for a customer under a written contract with the CPEO that meets the requirements of section 7705(e)(2), at a work site where at least 85 percent of the individuals performing services for the customer at that work site are subject to one or more such contracts with the CPEO, not counting excluded employees within the meaning of section 414(q)(5).


The IRS says a CPEO is generally solely liable for the customer’s employment taxes, returns, deposits and payments on the remuneration it pays to worksite employees. For remuneration the CPEO pays to employees who are not worksite employees, the IRS says the CPEO and its customer may both be liable.


A CPEO files aggregate employment tax returns under its own EIN and allocates each customer’s wages on Schedule R by the customer’s EIN. A CPEO contract must show the CPEO’s exact name and EIN, and the IRS publishes a list of certified CPEOs that it updates quarterly. Under Treasury Regulation 31.3511-1(f)(1)(ii), section 3511 does not apply to a customer whose CPEO contract has started but whose start has not been reported to the IRS. If a CPEO’s certification is revoked, the CPEO must tell its customers in writing that section 3511 no longer applies to the relationship and that customers may also be liable, as of the effective date of revocation, for federal employment taxes on pay the CPEO remits.
Can a contract change who is liable?
The IRS says liability is determined by the Internal Revenue Code and cannot be altered by a private agreement or contract between an employer and a third party. The same manual adds that a contract cannot release an employer from its responsibility to withhold, report and pay applicable employment taxes.


In its guidance to examiners on PEOs, the IRS says a client generally is not relieved of its employment tax obligation by using a PEO, and that the examiner should advise the client to use due diligence in selecting and continuing with a PEO.

With AsureWorks, Asure specialists do the work on AsureCentral and the client remains the employer, with statutory liability staying with the employer, which matches the IRS’s general rule that an employer who outsources payroll duties will generally remain responsible for them.
Which questions belong in writing?
Because the answers turn on the arrangement, these questions belong in writing before you sign.


* Ask whether the provider is a CPEO on the IRS list, and which exact legal name and EIN appear in the contract.
* Ask under whose EIN Forms 941, 940, W-2 and W-3 will be filed.
* Ask which IRS forms will be on file for you, such as Form 8655 for a reporting agent, Form 2678 for a section 3504 agent or Form 8973 for a CPEO, as the IRS third party arrangement chart lays them out.
* Ask whether the agreement says the provider asserts it is the employer, pays the wages and assumes responsibility for the taxes.
* Ask whether you will receive the reporting agent’s written statement at the start and at least quarterly, if the provider is a reporting agent.
* Ask how wages will be allocated to your EIN on Schedule R and how you will receive client-level reports, if the provider files aggregate returns.
* Ask what notice you will receive, and when, if certification is suspended, revoked or ended.
* Ask how you can verify deposits yourself and which address is on file with the IRS as your address of record.
* Ask what the base fee covers, which HR and benefits services are in scope, what the service levels are, how long implementation takes and what fees apply on exit.
Frequently asked questions
Who is the employer when I outsource payroll?
The IRS says an employer that outsources payroll and related tax duties to a third-party payer will generally remain responsible for those duties, including liability for the taxes, with an exception for certified professional employer organizations (CPEOs). A CPEO is treated as the employer of a worksite employee for federal employment taxes, but only for pay the CPEO remits to that employee.
Does payroll software change who the employer is?
The IRS test asks whether a business can control what work is done and how it is done, and the tool used to run payroll is not part of that question. An employer that runs its own payroll files its returns under its own EIN.
Can a provider be my employer for tax purposes?
A certified professional employer organization (CPEO) is treated as the employer of a worksite employee for federal employment taxes, but only for pay the CPEO remits to that employee. A payroll service provider or reporting agent works under the employer’s own EIN, and the IRS says neither is liable as an employer or an agent for the employer’s employment taxes. A PEO that is not a CPEO and meets the service-agreement definition in Treasury Regulation 31.3504-2 is designated to perform employer acts for the wages it pays, and the IRS says the PEO and its client are concurrently liable.
Who is responsible for hiring and firing when a CPEO is involved?
A CPEO contract that meets the requirements of section 7705(e)(2) of the Internal Revenue Code has the CPEO assume responsibility for recruiting, hiring and firing in addition to the customer’s responsibility for those tasks. The same contract is in writing and also has the CPEO assume responsibility for paying wages, for reporting, withholding and paying the taxes, for benefits the contract requires and for keeping employee records.
Does CPEO status decide every legal question about who my employer is?
CPEO treatment is a federal employment tax rule, and the statute limits its reach. Section 7705 says it is not to be read to affect who is an employee or employer for purposes of the Code, except as needed for section 3511, and Treasury Regulation 31.3511-1(b)(3) adds that the presumption in paragraph (b)(1), which looks to the customer’s type of employer for rules that depend on the type of employer, creates no inference about who is an employer or employee for federal tax purposes or for purposes of any other provision of law.
